title: Push and pull
stem: Which statement about magnets is correct?
key: A magnet can push or pull without touching. It pushes only another magnet.

options.text: A magnet must touch an object before it can pull it.
options.pick: Most pushes and pulls need touching.
options.why: A magnet pulls a steel paper clip from a short distance away, without touching it.

options.text: A magnet can push a steel paper clip away.
options.pick: Magnets push as well as pull, so they seem to push anything.
options.why: A magnet only pulls steel. It pushes only another magnet.

options.text: A magnet can push another magnet away, and pull a steel paper clip, without touching them.
options.pick: When does a magnet push, and when does it pull?
options.why: Like poles push apart, and a magnet pulls magnetic materials such as steel, without touching.

options.text: A magnet can pull a plastic cup towards it.
options.pick: Magnets seem to pull everything.
options.why: Plastic is not a magnetic material, so a magnet doesn't pull it.

title: A broken magnet
stem:
A bar magnet, with its N pole on the left and its S pole on the right, is broken into two pieces.

Which statement is correct?
key: If a magnet breaks, each piece is a magnet with its own N pole and S pole.

options.text: The left piece has only a N pole, and the right piece has only a S pole.
options.pick: Each piece keeps the pole it already had.
options.why: Each piece becomes a magnet with both a N pole and a S pole.

options.text: Each piece has a N pole and a S pole.
options.pick: Every magnet has two poles. Is each piece a magnet?
options.why: Each piece is a magnet, so each has a N pole and a S pole.

options.text: The broken ends have no poles.
options.pick: The new ends were in the middle, which seems not to be a pole.
options.why: The broken ends become new poles.

options.text: Neither piece is a magnet any more.
options.pick: Breaking seems to spoil the magnet.
options.why: Each piece is still a magnet, with two poles.

title: Paper clips on a magnet
stem:
A bar magnet is dipped into a box of steel paper clips and lifted out.

Where do most of the paper clips cling?
key: A magnet is strongest at its poles, at its two ends.

options.text: In the middle of the magnet
options.pick: The middle seems to be the centre of the magnet's strength.
options.why: A magnet is weakest in the middle. It is strongest at its poles.

options.text: Evenly all along the magnet
options.pick: The whole magnet seems to be equally magnetic.
options.why: Most clips cling to the ends, where the poles are.

options.text: Only at the N end
options.pick: The N pole seems to be the strong one.
options.why: Both poles are equally strong, so clips cling to both ends.

options.text: At both ends
options.pick: Where is a magnet strongest?
options.why: A magnet is strongest at its poles, at its two ends.

title: What will a magnet attract?
stem: Which pair of objects will a magnet attract?
key: A magnet attracts iron and steel. Aluminium, copper and plastic are not attracted.

options.text: A steel paper clip and an iron nail
options.pick: Which objects are made of iron or steel?
options.why: Iron and steel are magnetic materials, so a magnet attracts both.

options.text: An iron nail and an aluminium can
options.pick: Both are metal.
options.why: Aluminium is not a magnetic material, so the can is not attracted.

options.text: A copper wire and a steel paper clip
options.pick: Both are metal.
options.why: Copper is not a magnetic material.

options.text: A plastic ruler and an iron nail
options.pick: Plastic rulers seem light enough to be pulled.
options.why: Plastic is not a magnetic material.

title: Magnet or steel bar?
stem:
Ali has a magnet and a steel bar that look exactly the same. He brings each one, in turn, close to the N pole of another magnet.

Which result tells him which one is the magnet?
key: Only a magnet can be repelled. Repelling is the sure test for a magnet.

options.text: The one that is attracted is the magnet.
options.pick: Magnets attract each other.
options.why: The steel bar is attracted too, so being attracted doesn't tell them apart.

options.text: The one that is not attracted is the magnet.
options.pick: Two magnets seem to cancel each other out.
options.why: Two magnets always push or pull each other.

options.text: The one that is repelled at one end is the magnet.
options.pick: Which result can only happen between two magnets?
options.why: Only a magnet can be repelled. Its N pole is pushed away by the other N pole.

options.text: The steel bar is the one that is repelled.
options.pick: Steel seems to react strongly to magnets.
options.why: Steel is only ever attracted. It is never repelled.

title: What magnets are made of
stem: Which material can a magnet be made of?
key: Magnets can be made of iron or steel.

options.text: Aluminium
options.pick: Aluminium is a metal.
options.why: Aluminium is not a magnetic material, so it cannot be made into a magnet.

options.text: Copper
options.pick: Copper is a metal used with electricity.
options.why: Copper is not a magnetic material.

options.text: Steel
options.pick: Which material is magnetic?
options.why: Magnets can be made of iron or steel.

options.text: Plastic
options.pick: Fridge magnets have plastic on the outside.
options.why: The plastic is only a cover. The magnet inside is iron or steel.

title: The stroke method
stem:
Siti wants to make a steel needle into a magnet by stroking it with a bar magnet.

Which way is correct?
key: Stroke many times, in the same direction, with the same pole.

options.text: Stroke it back and forth along its length, many times
options.pick: More rubbing seems to give more magnetism.
options.why: Stroking back and forth undoes the work. Stroke in one direction only.

options.text: Stroke it with the N pole, then the S pole, in turn
options.pick: Using both poles seems fair.
options.why: Use the same pole every time.

options.text: Stroke it once, very hard
options.pick: A hard stroke seems stronger.
options.why: It needs many strokes, not one hard one.

options.text: Stroke it many times, in the same direction, with the same pole
options.pick: Recall the three "same" and "many" rules.
options.why: Many strokes, in the same direction, with the same pole, turn the steel into a magnet.

title: An electromagnet
stem:
An iron nail with a coil of wire is connected to one battery. The number of coils was changed, and the paper clips the nail picked up were counted.

What do the results show?
figure:
Number of coilsPaper clips picked up
104
208
3012
key: More coils of wire make an electromagnet stronger.

options.text: More coils make the magnet stronger.
options.pick: What happens to the number of clips as the coils go up?
options.why: More coils picked up more clips, so the magnet got stronger.

options.text: Fewer coils make the magnet stronger.
options.pick: Less wire seems to let the battery work better.
options.why: The 10-coil nail picked up the fewest clips.

options.text: The number of coils does not change how strong the magnet is.
options.pick: It is the same nail and the same battery.
options.why: The clips went from 4 to 12, so the coils did change the strength.

options.text: The magnet is strongest with 20 coils, the middle number.
options.pick: The middle seems a safe choice.
options.why: 30 coils picked up the most clips.

title: A fridge door
stem:
A fridge door stays shut because a magnet in the door seal is attracted to the fridge's frame.

What could the frame be made of?
key: A magnet attracts steel, so a fridge frame made of steel holds the door shut.

options.text: Aluminium
options.pick: Fridges are made of metal.
options.why: Aluminium is not attracted by a magnet.

options.text: Steel
options.pick: What does a magnet attract?
options.why: Steel is a magnetic material, so the magnet in the seal is attracted to it.

options.text: Plastic
options.pick: The inside of a fridge is plastic.
options.why: A magnet does not attract plastic.

options.text: Any metal
options.pick: All metals seem to stick to magnets.
options.why: Only iron and steel are attracted. Aluminium and copper are not.

title: At the recycling centre
stem:
A big magnet lifts the steel cans out of a pile of steel and aluminium cans.

Which statement explains this?
key: Steel is a magnetic material and aluminium is not.

options.text: The magnet attracts both kinds of can, but the aluminium cans fall off.
options.pick: All cans are metal.
options.why: The magnet does not attract aluminium at all.

options.text: The magnet has to touch each can before it can lift it.
options.pick: Lifting seems to need touching.
options.why: A magnet pulls steel cans from a short distance away.

options.text: The magnet pushes the aluminium cans away.
options.pick: The aluminium cans are left behind, so they seem to be pushed.
options.why: A magnet neither pulls nor pushes aluminium. The cans just stay where they are.

options.text: The magnet attracts steel but not aluminium.
options.pick: Which of the two metals is magnetic?
options.why: Steel is a magnetic material and aluminium is not, so only the steel cans are lifted.

title: Which one sticks?
stem: Which object would a magnet attract?
key: A magnet attracts objects made of iron or steel.

options.text: A sheet of aluminium foil
options.pick: Foil is metal.
options.why: Aluminium is not a magnetic material.

options.text: A copper wire
options.pick: Wires are metal.
options.why: Copper is not a magnetic material.

options.text: A wooden spoon
options.pick: It is light.
options.why: Wood is not a magnetic material.

options.text: A steel spoon
options.pick: Which one is made of a magnetic material?
options.why: Steel is a magnetic material.

title: A can that does not stick
stem:
Mei holds a magnet close to a metal drink can. The can is not attracted.

What can she tell from this?
key: Not every metal is magnetic. Only iron and steel are attracted.

options.text: The can is not made of iron or steel. It could be aluminium.
options.pick: Which metals does a magnet attract?
options.why: Only iron and steel are attracted, so the can must be another metal, such as aluminium.

options.text: The can must be plastic, because every metal is attracted.
options.pick: Metal seems always to stick.
options.why: Not every metal is magnetic. An aluminium can is metal and is not attracted.

options.text: The magnet must touch the can before it can pull it.
options.pick: Pulling seems to need touching.
options.why: A magnet pulls steel without touching. This can isn't steel.

options.text: The can must be steel that has been pushed away.
options.pick: Something stopped it sticking.
options.why: A magnet never pushes steel away.

title: A nail that did not work
stem:
Ravi stroked an iron nail back and forth with a magnet many times, but it did not become a magnet.

What should he do?
key: Stroke in one direction only, many times, with the same pole.

options.text: Stroke it with the N pole and the S pole in turn.
options.pick: Using both poles seems to help.
options.why: Use the same pole every time.

options.text: Stroke it in one direction only, many times, with the same pole.
options.pick: What did he do wrong?
options.why: Stroking back and forth undoes the magnetism. Stroke one way only, with one pole.

options.text: Stroke it fewer times.
options.pick: Too much stroking seems to wear it out.
options.why: It needs many strokes, in one direction.

options.text: Use an aluminium rod instead.
options.pick: A different metal might work better.
options.why: Aluminium cannot be made into a magnet at all.

title: What can be made into a magnet?
stem: Which object can be made into a magnet by stroking it with a magnet?
key: Only iron and steel can be made into magnets.

options.text: A copper wire
options.pick: It is a metal.
options.why: Copper is not a magnetic material.

options.text: A plastic straw
options.pick: It is long and thin, like a needle.
options.why: Plastic is not a magnetic material.

options.text: A steel knitting needle
options.pick: Which one is made of a magnetic material?
options.why: Steel can be made into a magnet.

options.text: An aluminium rod
options.pick: It is a metal rod, like a bar magnet.
options.why: Aluminium is not a magnetic material.

title: More batteries
stem:
An iron nail with 20 coils of wire was connected to one battery, then to two batteries. The paper clips it picked up were counted.

What do the results show?
figure:
Number of batteriesPaper clips picked up
15
210
key: More batteries make an electromagnet stronger.

options.text: Fewer batteries make the magnet stronger.
options.pick: Fewer batteries seem gentler on the nail.
options.why: One battery picked up fewer clips.

options.text: Only the number of coils changes the strength, not the batteries.
options.pick: The coils seem to be what makes the magnet.
options.why: The coils stayed at 20, and the clips doubled with the batteries.

options.text: The number of clips depends only on the size of the nail.
options.pick: A bigger nail seems to hold more clips.
options.why: The nail was the same. Only the batteries changed.

options.text: More batteries make the magnet stronger.
options.pick: What happened to the clips when a battery was added?
options.why: Two batteries picked up more clips than one, so the magnet was stronger.

title: A fair coil test
stem:
Ali wants to find out if the number of coils affects how strong his electromagnet is.

What should he change?
key: Change only the thing you are testing. Keep everything else the same.

options.text: Only the number of coils
options.pick: What is he trying to find out about?
options.why: Change only the coils, and keep the batteries, the nail and the clips the same.

options.text: Only the number of batteries
options.pick: Batteries also change the strength.
options.why: That tests batteries, not coils.

options.text: Both the coils and the batteries
options.pick: Changing more seems to give clearer results.
options.why: If both change, he can't tell which one made the difference.

options.text: The size of the nail
options.pick: The nail is part of the magnet.
options.why: That tests the nail, not the coils.

title: Counting clips along a magnet
stem:
Paper clips clinging to a bar magnet were counted. The results are shown.

Which statement is correct?
figure:
Part of the magnetPaper clips clinging
end A8
middle1
end B8
key: A magnet is strongest at its poles, at its two ends.

options.text: The magnet is strongest in the middle.
options.pick: The middle is the centre of the magnet.
options.why: Only 1 clip clung to the middle.

options.text: The magnet is strongest at its poles, at the ends.
options.pick: Where did most clips cling?
options.why: 8 clips clung to each end, where the poles are.

options.text: The magnet is equally strong all along.
options.pick: It is one piece of steel.
options.why: The ends held 8 clips, and the middle held only 1.

options.text: Only end A is a pole.
options.pick: End A is named first.
options.why: End B held as many clips as end A. Both ends are poles.

title: A horseshoe magnet
stem:
A horseshoe magnet is dipped into paper clips.

Where do most of the clips cling?
key: A magnet is strongest at its poles. A horseshoe magnet's poles are its two ends.

options.text: At the bend in the middle
options.pick: The bend is the biggest part.
options.why: The bend is the middle of the magnet, where it is weakest.

options.text: Evenly all over
options.pick: The whole magnet seems equally magnetic.
options.why: Most clips cling to the poles.

options.text: At its two ends
options.pick: Where are the poles of a horseshoe magnet?
options.why: Its poles are its two ends, where it is strongest.

options.text: At one end only
options.pick: Only one end seems to be the pole.
options.why: Every magnet has two poles, so clips cling to both ends.

title: Cutting a magnet into three
stem:
A bar magnet is cut into three pieces.

How many poles does the middle piece have?
key: Every piece of a magnet is a magnet with two poles.

options.text: Two: a N pole and a S pole
options.pick: Is the middle piece a magnet?
options.why: Every piece of a magnet is a magnet with two poles.

options.text: None, because the middle of a magnet is not magnetic
options.pick: The middle of a magnet picks up few clips.
options.why: Once it is cut, the middle piece has its own two ends, and they are poles.

options.text: One
options.pick: It came from between two poles.
options.why: A magnet always has two poles.

options.text: It depends on how long the piece is.
options.pick: Short pieces seem too small to have poles.
options.why: Every piece has two poles, however short it is.

title: A toy car rolls away
stem:
A toy car has a magnet fixed to its back. When another magnet is brought close, without touching, the car rolls away.

Why?
key: Like poles repel, even without touching.

options.text: Unlike poles are facing each other, so they repel.
options.pick: Pushing seems to go with "different".
options.why: Unlike poles attract. Like poles repel.

options.text: Like poles are facing each other, so they repel.
options.pick: Which poles push each other apart?
options.why: Like poles repel, so the car is pushed away.

options.text: The magnet must have touched the car.
options.pick: Pushing seems to need touching.
options.why: Magnets push and pull without touching.

options.text: The steel body of the car is repelled by the magnet.
options.pick: The car is metal.
options.why: A magnet never repels steel. Only the magnet on the car can be repelled.

title: A magnetic train
stem:
A magnetic train floats above its track because magnets in the train and track push each other apart.

Which poles must face each other?
key: Like poles repel.

options.text: Unlike poles, such as N facing S
options.pick: Opposite seems to mean pushing away.
options.why: Unlike poles attract. They would pull the train down.

options.text: Any poles, because magnets always push
options.pick: Magnets seem to push each other.
options.why: Magnets push only when like poles face each other.

options.text: No poles: the track does the pushing
options.pick: The track seems to hold the train up.
options.why: The push comes from like poles of magnets in the train and track.

options.text: Like poles, such as N facing N
options.pick: Which poles push apart?
options.why: Like poles repel, so the train is pushed up.

title: A cupboard catch
stem:
A cupboard door is held shut by a small magnet in the frame, which pulls on a plate fixed to the door.

What could the plate be made of?
key: A magnet pulls on iron and steel.

options.text: Aluminium
options.pick: It is a metal plate.
options.why: Aluminium is not attracted by a magnet.

options.text: Plastic
options.pick: Plastic plates are common.
options.why: Plastic is not attracted by a magnet.

options.text: Steel
options.pick: What does a magnet pull on?
options.why: Steel is a magnetic material, so the magnet holds it.

options.text: Wood
options.pick: The door is wood.
options.why: Wood is not attracted by a magnet.
